clinicalPearls: A benign tumour of hair-follicle matrix differentiation, most common in children and young adults on the head, neck, and upper limbs
Presents as a firm, sometimes stony-hard, mobile subcutaneous nodule, occasionally with a bluish or reddish hue through the overlying skin
Stretching the overlying skin can reveal multiple facets and angulated edges, the so-called tent sign, reflecting internal calcification
Driven by activating mutations of CTNNB1 leading to beta-catenin stabilisation and aberrant Wnt signalling in the follicular matrix
Histology shows basaloid matrix cells maturing into anucleate eosinophilic shadow (ghost) cells, with dystrophic calcification and often foreign-body giant-cell reaction and ossification
Usually solitary; multiple lesions may prompt consideration of associations such as myotonic dystrophy and other syndromes
Treatment is simple surgical excision, which is curative; malignant transformation (pilomatrix carcinoma) is rare
reference.pathophysiology: Pilomatricoma is a benign neoplasm derived from the matrix cells of the hair follicle. Activating mutations in CTNNB1, the gene encoding beta-catenin, prevent its normal degradation, so stabilised beta-catenin accumulates and constitutively activates Wnt signalling, driving proliferation of follicular matrix cells. These basaloid cells progressively lose their nuclei as they differentiate, producing sheets of eosinophilic anucleate shadow (ghost) cells. Over time the lesion undergoes dystrophic calcification and sometimes true ossification, with a surrounding foreign-body giant-cell and granulomatous reaction, accounting for the characteristic firm to stony consistency.
additionalDifferentials: Basal cell carcinoma (when ulcerated or facial)
additionalInvestigations: Clinical examination for the tent sign and stony consistency
Skin ultrasound showing a well-defined nodule with internal calcification and acoustic shadowing
Excisional biopsy with histopathology demonstrating shadow cells and calcification
Immunohistochemistry for nuclear beta-catenin in equivocal cases
Evaluation for associated syndromes when lesions are multiple (e.g. myotonic dystrophy)
redFlags: Rapid enlargement, ulceration, or infiltrative growth suggesting pilomatrix carcinoma
Multiple pilomatricomas prompting evaluation for an underlying syndrome
Recurrence after excision raising concern for incomplete removal or malignancy
reference.prognosis: Pilomatricoma is benign with an excellent prognosis; complete excision is curative and recurrence is uncommon. The rare malignant counterpart, pilomatrix carcinoma, can recur locally and occasionally metastasise.
pitfalls: Mistaking the firm nodule for an epidermoid cyst or calcified lymph node and mismanaging it
Failing to recognise the tent sign and characteristic clinical features
Overlooking multiple lesions that may signal an associated systemic disorder
Dismissing atypical rapidly growing lesions that could represent malignant transformation
management: Pilomatricoma is managed as a benign lesion in the great majority of cases
For a typical firm, mobile, slow-growing nodule, complete surgical excision is diagnostic and curative and no systemic staging or oncology referral is needed
Clinical observation with interval follow-up is a reasonable alternative for small, asymptomatic, cosmetically acceptable lesions when the lesion stays indolent and stable
Rapidly enlarging, ulcerated, fixed, or infiltrative lesions should raise suspicion for the rare malignant counterpart, pilomatrix carcinoma, and prompt wider excision and closer surveillance
For lesions concerning for pilomatrix carcinoma, wide local excision with attention to margin clearance is preferred over simple excision
All excised specimens, even clinically typical ones, should undergo histopathology to confirm the diagnosis and exclude malignant transformation
There is no established role for radiotherapy or systemic chemotherapy or targeted therapy in benign pilomatricoma, since surgery alone is curative in most cases
For pilomatrix carcinoma with nodal or distant spread, management follows a multidisciplinary case-by-case approach analogous to other cutaneous adnexal carcinomas, without a standardized regimen
Routine long-term oncologic surveillance is not required after excision of a classic benign lesion beyond standard post-surgical wound follow-up
Lesions excised with atypical features, or confirmed pilomatrix carcinoma, warrant closer follow-up for local recurrence with imaging and nodal assessment as clinically indicated
Multiple pilomatricomas should prompt evaluation for associated syndromic conditions such as myotonic dystrophy
Refer to dermatology or general or plastic surgery for excisional biopsy of any suspected pilomatricoma
Refer to surgical oncology and consider a multidisciplinary tumour board for lesions with features concerning for pilomatrix carcinoma
Refer for genetic or syndromic evaluation when pilomatricomas are multiple, particularly with possible myotonic dystrophy
